cues.text: The client's system says every order goes:
release, pick, consolidate, pack, check, ship.
You open the log.
Fifty-four percent do.
Why do the rest find thirty other ways?
That's the fog.
So before any analysis, you define the decision:
cut the waiting in half, at one site, in twelve weeks.
If it matters, it can be observed.
If it can be observed, it can be measured.
Three people arrive with the same problem.
One writes a fifty-page deck.
It's good.
Nothing changes.
One builds the perfect dashboard.
Nobody opens it.
The third sees it like an anthropologist, a psychologist,
a historian, and brings an engineer.
You don't ask what they would want.
You ask for the last time it went wrong.
You watch what they do, not what they say.
Then the floor answers:
a hundred and fifty-seven meters walked per order.
Then you doubt.
A quarter of the products have bad data,
give or take five points, checked on the floor,
not on the screen.
AI drafts the analysis,
and someone on your side is paid to argue against it.
You draw the system, not the org chart.
Sixty-one percent of the wait sits in one queue.
You ask what incentive, or what structure, keeps it there.
The operators hear automation, and feel replacement.
A team is not a list of people.
You name the fear, without judgment, and wait.
The director gets the answer first, on one page.
You test the riskiest assumption first, in one zone,
with a control group agreed in advance.
A meeting only counts if someone commits to something.
And you ask:
can we, should we, who does it affect?
In nineteen fifty-one,
coal miners showed that changing the machine can break the team.
At week twelve you leave a runbook, and signed sheets.
Success is what they do without you.
One person.
Many disciplines.
One map.
Where the rules are clear, let the machine win.
Where there are none, you are there.
And when you leave, the map stays.
